title: Buffers, splits and tabs
summary: Work on several files in one vim: buffers, windows and tab pages.

steps.title: Three ideas
body: - A **buffer** is a file loaded in memory. `vim a.txt b.txt` opens two buffers.
- A **window** is a view onto a buffer. Splits show several windows at once.
- A **tab page** is a layout of windows (not one tab per file, as in browsers).
:e other.conf     edit another file in this window
:b 3   :b conf    switch to buffer 3, or by part of its name
Ctrl+W w          cycle windows;  Ctrl+W h/j/k/l  move to the window in that direction
Ctrl+W q  or :q   close the window
:tabnew file      new tab page;  gt / gT  next / previous tab
> **Practise:** open **Labs → Vim & nano trainer** and run this lesson's challenges until the keys come without thinking.

steps.prompt: Match the command to what it does.
pairs: show the next buffer in this window
open app.conf in a vertical split
move to the window on the right
go to the next tab page
write every changed buffer and quit

steps.prompt: You have 3 splits open and type `:q`. What happens?
options: Only the current window closes; vim keeps running with 2
steps.explain: `:q` closes a window; vim exits when the last one closes. `:qa` closes them all.

steps.prompt: Order the commands: open `nginx.conf`, split it vertically with `site.conf`, move back to the left window, then save both and quit.
Compare two files side by side and move between them.

steps.title: The alternate file
steps.body: `Ctrl+^` (Ctrl+6) jumps between the current and the previous buffer, the fastest way to flip between two files. `:e #` does the same. If the buffer has unsaved changes vim refuses with `E37`; either `:w` first or `:set hidden` (default in neovim) so buffers can stay modified in the background.

steps.title: Rename across files: :vimgrep and :cfdo
prompt: Rename the class `OldClient` to `NewClient` in **every `.cs` file** under `~/proj`, as a whole word. `OldClientTests` and `OldClientOptions` keep their names, and `README.md` must not change.
Vim's multi-file workflow: `:vimgrep` fills the **quickfix list** with every match, and `:cfdo` runs a command once in each file of that list:
:cfdo %s/\<OldClient\>/NewClient/g | update    replace, and save each changed buffer
In full-screen Vim you would look at the list with `:copen` first. Here, run both from `~/proj` with `vim -es -c '...' -c '...' -c qa`.

checks.name: no whole-word OldClient is left in .cs files
checks.fail: These lines still have `OldClient` as a whole word:

checks.name: every one became NewClient
checks.fail: The number of `NewClient` does not match the number of `OldClient` you started with. Did something else get renamed, or a file get missed?

checks.name: OldClientTests and OldClientOptions keep their names
checks.cmd: cd ~/proj && rg -q 'class OldClientTests' tests/OldClientTests.cs && rg -q 'OldClientOptions' src/Billing/Invoices.cs
checks.fail: A longer name that only starts with `OldClient` was changed. `\<OldClient\>` matches the whole word only.

hints: Start in `~/proj`: `**/*.cs` is relative to the current folder.
`:vimgrep /\<OldClient\>/ **/*.cs` then `:cfdo %s/\<OldClient\>/NewClient/g | update`. `update` writes only buffers that changed.
steps.explain: `:cfdo` runs once per file in the quickfix list (`:cdo` once per match, so it needs the `e` flag on `:s` when a line has two hits). The file `OldClient.cs` keeps its name: renaming files is a job for `git mv`, and a language server's rename (VS Code F2) would do both and fix the references the text search cannot see.
